title: MedFusion-gP-AKI: development and multicenter validation of a machine learning fusion model for early prediction of KDIGO stage 3 acute kidney injury in critically ill traumatic cervicothoracic spinal cord injury patients

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《MedFusion-gP-AKI: development and multicenter validation of a machine learning fusion model for early prediction of KDIGO stage 3 acute kidney injury in critically ill traumatic cervicothoracic spinal cord injury patients》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · S0001-p1】Critically ill traumatic cervicothoracic spinal cord injury (TCTSCI) patients often develop neurogenic shock due to abrupt sympathetic dysfunction, leading to systemic vasodilation, arterial hypoperfusion, and inadequate multiorgan perfusion, which rapidly reduces renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in the early phase [1]. Simultaneously, the systemic inflammatory response extends beyond the injured spinal cord to distant organs such as the kidneys, characterized by early immune cell infiltration and sustained proinflammatory cytokine expression, further aggravating kidney injury under impaired microcirculation [2]. This combined impact of hemodynamic collapse and immune-mediated inflammation contributes to the high incidence of acute kidney injury (AKI), a common and critical complication in TCTSCI [3]. Galeiras et al. [4] reported that over half of traumatic spinal cord injury (TSCI) patients develop AKI early after injury, with even higher rates in critically ill cases, while KDIGO (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes) stage 3 AKI has been independently linked to poor short-term outcomes and, as further reported by Yu et al. [5] serves as a predictor of failure to discontinue mechanical ventilation in patients with high cervical injury, highlighting the pivotal role of early kidney dysfunction in clinical management and short-term prognosis in critically ill TCTSCI patients.

【Introduction · S0001-p2】Furthermore, in critically ill TCTSCI patients, AKI may pose long-term health risks beyond the acute phase, as residual kidney damage, even after a partial recovery, easily tends to progress to chronic kidney disease (CKD), which, in the context of TCTSCI, further disrupts blood pressure regulation and markedly increases cardiovascular risk [6]. Given that cardiovascular complications are the leading cause of late mortality in chronic TCTSCI, the prevention of secondary organ dysfunction, particularly kidney impairment, is considered as important as promoting neurological recovery in improving long-term survival and quality of life [7].

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《MedFusion-gP-AKI: development and multicenter validation of a machine learning fusion model for early prediction of KDIGO stage 3 acute kidney injury in critically ill traumatic cervicothoracic spinal cord injury patients》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Comparative performance of baseline models · S0003-S2004-p1】All models underwent hyperparameter tuning via five-fold cross-validated optimization on both the original and SMOTified-GAN training cohorts, with the tuned parameters summarized in Supplementary Table 1. On the original, highly imbalanced dataset, all models showed limited discrimination, fragile calibration, and minimal net clinical benefit, with detailed results provided in Supplementary Material 2. Using SMOTified-GAN, the number of critically ill TCTSCI patients with KGIGO stage 3 AKI increased from 140 to 919, balanced against 856 without stage 3 AKI. Across both the training (Figure 4a–4f) and internal validation (Figure 5a–5f) sets, the fifteen candidate models exhibited heterogeneous performance in discrimination (Figure 4a/5a), precision-recall metrics (Figure 4b/5b), net clinical benefit (Figure 4c/5c), calibration (Figure 4d/5d), gain-based ranking (Figure 4e/5e), and radar-based composite evaluation (Figure 4f/5f). TabNet demonstrated relatively strong performance with AUCs of 0.879 and 0.853 and APs of 0.878 and 0.867 across training and internal validation, ranking highly on ROC and PR curves while maintaining close alignment between predicted and observed risks in calibration, delivering net clinical benefit across most threshold intervals, and exhibiting a sharply rising gain curve that indicated robust capacity to identify true positives within the top 20% high-risk population. NODE and DKL yielded comparably stable results across both training and internal validation cohorts, with NODE achieving AUCs of 0.867 and 0.873 and APs of 0.872 and 0.873, and DKL reaching AUCs of 0.879 and 0.871 with APs of 0.859 and 0.879, all reflecting reliable discrimination, calibration consistency, and stratification capacity across both cohorts. SAINT maintained balanced AUC and AP values of 0.862 and 0.865 and 0.848 and 0.863, respectively, with calibration deviations confined to the mid-probability range and moderate gain performance. RF and FT-Transformer showed high scores during training but experienced marked degradation in validation, with AUCs declining to 0.812 and 0.811 and APs to 0.813 and 0.802, respectively, suggesting potential overfitting as corroborated by flatter gain slopes and radar plots indicating suboptimal specificity and precision. Classical algorithms, including logistic regression, LightGBM, SVM, GBM, CatBoost, and MLP, generally produced AUC and AP values ranging from 0.7 to 0.8, yet their net benefit often approximated the treat-none baseline under medium to high thresholds, with shallow gain curves and no evident advantage in accuracy, sensitivity, or F1 score. KNN displayed considerable performance fluctuation, with AUCs of 0.854 and 0.693 and APs of 0.817 and 0.711, accompanied by unstable calibration and inconsistent gain. XGBoost ranked consistently lowest across nearly all evaluation metrics, including AUCs of 0.763 and 0.710 and APs of 0.742 and 0.716, and exhibited poor discrimination, limited clinical utility, and compact radar plot patterns.

【Performance of MedFusion-GP-AKI models · S0003-S2005-p3】In the pre-SMOTE training cohort, MedFusion-GP-AKI achieved an AUC of 0.938 and an AP of 0.841, indicating strong discrimination even before class rebalancing, with the pre-SMOTE internal validation set showing comparable performance (AUC = 0.900; AP = 0.838). Following SMOTE augmentation, both the training (AUC = 0.969; AP = 0.992) and internal validation (AUC = 0.945; AP = 0.927) sets demonstrated modest improvement in sensitivity within high-recall regions, consistent with enhanced minority-class representation rather than overfitting. Importantly, the external cohort maintained robust discriminative capacity (AUC = 0.921; AP = 0.878), confirming that model performance generalized well across independent institutions (Figure 6a and 6b).

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《MedFusion-gP-AKI: development and multicenter validation of a machine learning fusion model for early prediction of KDIGO stage 3 acute kidney injury in critically ill traumatic cervicothoracic spinal cord injury patients》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Figure 1. · F0001】Figure 1. Study workflow for the development, validation, and interpretation of the MedFusion-GP-AKI model for predicting KIDGO stage 3 AKI in critically ill TCTSCI patients.From 1,046 patients identified in the MIMIC-IV and eICU databases, 996 were retained after excluding those younger than 18 years or with excessive missing data. These patients were categorized into non-AKI (n = 406), stage 1 (n = 152), stage 2 (n = 298), and stage 3 (n = 140), yielding 856 non–stage 3 and 140 stage 3 AKI cases. The pre-SMOTE dataset was divided into a training set of 697 patients (98 stage 3 AKI and 599 non–stage 3 AKI) and a test set of 299 patients (42 stage 3 AKI and 257 non–stage 3 AKI) for baseline evaluation. To address class imbalance, a SMOTified-GAN was then applied to generate synthetic stage 3 AKI samples, resulting in a balanced dataset of 1,712 patients. This balanced dataset was further divided into a training cohort of 1,198 patients (633 stage 3 AKI and 565 non–stage 3 AKI) and a test cohort of 514 patients (288 stage 3 AKI and 286 non–stage 3 AKI) for model development and validation. Subsequently, feature selection integrating VIB, ACAE, and NOTEARS was performed to identify clinically relevant predictors. Fifteen machine learning models, including XGBoost, TabNet, SVM, RF, SAINT, NODE, LR, LightGBM, KNN, GBM, DKL, FT Transformer, CatBoost, AdaBoost, and MLP, were then trained and evaluated on both the original imbalanced dataset and the SMOTified-GAN balanced dataset through ROC, calibration, precision–recall, decision-curve, and gain-curve analyses, together with accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1 metrics. Models with relatively superior performance were subsequently integrated into the MedFusion-GP-AKI ensemble, which was validated across both the original and balanced datasets in their respective training and validation cohorts, and further evaluated in an external cohort of 188 critically ill TCTSCI patients from four tertiary hospitals in China (67 stage 3 AKI and 121 non–stage 3 AKI). Model interpretation and clinical deployment were supported by SHAP analysis and a web-based risk calculator.

【Figure 2. · F0002】Figure 2. Sixty-day Kaplan–Meier survival curves stratified by KDIGO AKI severity in critically ill TCTSCI patients.Kaplan–Meier survival analysis demonstrating the cumulative probability of survival within 60 days among critically ill TCTSCI patients stratified by KDIGO AKI severity. Patients without AKI exhibited the highest survival probability throughout the observation period, followed by those with stage 1 and stage 2 AKI, whereas patients with stage 3 AKI showed a markedly reduced survival probability with an early and steep decline within the first two weeks that continued to diverge over time. The overall differences across groups were statistically significant (log-rank test, p < 0.0001).

【Figure 3. · F0003】Figure 3. Feature selection in critically ill TCTSCI patients for stage 3 AKI prediction.(a) Variables identified by the VIB method are presented as a radar chart depicting the relative contributions of candidate predictors to outcome discrimination; (b) Features selected through the NOTEARS algorithm, illustrated by a causal graph highlighting direct and indirect associations with stage 3 AKI; (c) Predictors identified by the ACAE approach, ranked by counterfactual contribution and mean absolute shifts; (d) Integration of the three feature selection methods, with overlap indicating consensus predictors across VIB, NOTEARS, and ACAE; (e) Correlation heatmap illustrating inter-variable relationships among the selected features; (f) Variance inflation factor (VIF) analysis confirming the absence of multicollinearity among key predictors.

sections.title: 复现线索
sections.text:
《MedFusion-gP-AKI: development and multicenter validation of a machine learning fusion model for early prediction of KDIGO stage 3 acute kidney injury in critically ill traumatic cervicothoracic spinal cord injury patients》：复现时可直接核对的数据、软件或实现线索。

【Data availability statement · S0010-p1】The MIMIC-IV (version 3.1) and eICU Collaborative Research Database (version 2.0) are publicly available from the PhysioNet repository (https://physionet.org/) following credentialed access approval. Clinical data collected from the First Affiliated Hospital of Xinjiang Medical University, the People’s Hospital of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Chongqing University Three Gorges Hospital, as well as Jingzhou First People’s Hospital, which were fully de-identified prior to analysis, have been deposited as an anonymized external validation dataset in Zenodo and are publicly available at DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.17385515. Model-related information can be found on GitHub (https://github.com/Numwyx/MedFusion-GP-AKI).

【Statistical analysis and model development · S0002-S2006-p2】Machine learning modeling and interpretability analyses were conducted in Python 3.8.10 (Python Software Foundation, Delaware, USA), following the TRIPOD-AI and PROBAST-AI guidelines to ensure comprehensive adherence to best practices in the development, validation, transparent reporting, and risk-of-bias assessment of artificial intelligence–based predictive models [22,23]. Modeling was performed using both the original and SMOTified-GAN balanced datasets, each randomly partitioned into training and internal validation sets at a 7:3 ratio. A total of fifteen individual models were evaluated, including eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Tabular Network (TabNet), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), Self-Attention and Intersample Attention Transformer (SAINT), Neural Oblivious Decision Ensemble (NODE), Logistic Regression (LR), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), Feature Tokenizer Transformer (FT-Transformer), Deep Kernel Learning (DKL), Categorical Boosting (CatBoost), Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). Each model underwent hyperparameter optimization via five-fold cross-validation. Performance was comprehensively assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves with corresponding area under the curve (AUC), precision–recall (PR) curves with average precision (AP), calibration curves, decision curve analysis (DCA), and gain curves, with additional evaluation at a classification threshold of 0.5 using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1 score.
